Trump was hitting China with tariffs at the rate of almost one a week during the height of the trade war, and companies like Logitech immediately raised US prices significantly.

Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court ruled those tariffs illegal, requiring refunds to manufacturers. However, no company has yet passed on refunds to consumers, and a class-action lawsuit is now seeking to change that …

Trump tariff drama

Last year, Trump seized on the massive US trade deficit with China, apparently fantasizing that slapping huge tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to relocate production to the US.

In reality, this was always impossible. The US lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, specialist expertise, and cheap labor needed to support mass production of consumer electronics.

Trump kept insisting China would pay the tariffs, but the reality was that the cost fell entirely on US brands importing finished goods from China, with the additional cost passed on to consumers through price hikes. Tariffs peaked at 145% at one point.

Logitech, for example, raised prices on roughly half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers deserve refunds

The US Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that US businesses must be refunded the amounts they paid. That process is now underway.

The issue is that these costs were ultimately passed on to consumers through higher prices, but so far no affected company has shown any intention of refunding customers.

Law firm CPM has now filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech specifically, seeking to recover refunds for consumers who paid higher prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac opinion

The principle here is indisputable. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and are now being refunded by the government. Morally, they should refund consumers the relevant portion for purchases made during that period.

In practical terms, though, this would be extremely difficult to execute. Logitech would need to identify every transaction made through a vast network of third-party retailers, track what price consumers paid, and calculate the proportion attributable to tariffs.

Even if this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it might establish a very interesting precedent — though we have to note that the ones who typically profit from class-action lawsuits are the lawyers, with consumers on average receiving very small payouts.
